STONE AGE TO IRON AGE BRITAIN (c. 800,000 BC–AD 43) LESSON 1 OF 6 • CLASSROOM READING TEXT
LESSON 1 • Chronology & Change Over Time

Ice Age Hunters & Sunken Doggerland (c. 800,000–4000 BC)

Key Enquiry: How did Stone Age hunters survive—and how did Britain become an island?
[1.1] c. 850,000–10,000 BC: Ice Age Caves, Flint Handaxes & Mammoth Hunters
“How did Old Stone Age families survive the freezing Ice Age?”

Long before books, early humans lived during prehistory. Around 850,000 BC, barefoot families left footprints in wet mud at Happisburgh [HAPSB-ruh] in Norfolk. During the Palaeolithic [pal-ee-oh-LITH-ik], or Old Stone Age, thick Ice Age snow covered northern Britain. Families sheltered inside deep limestone caves like Creswell Crags.

Nobody had metal yet, so makers chipped sharp flint flakes by knapping. They shaped tear-drop handaxes to chop meat and wood. Brave teams tracked giant woolly mammoths for meat, warm hides, lamp fat, and bones.

[1.2] c. 10,000–7000 BC: Warming Forests, Cheddar Man & Star Carr
“How did warming forests change Mesolithic life after 10,000 BC?”

Around 10,000 BC, the Ice Age ended and the Mesolithic [mez-oh-LITH-ik], or Middle Stone Age, began. Green forests spread with red deer, wild boar, and hazelnuts. Small hunter-gatherer groups moved camp each season to fish rivers and pick berries. Inside Gough's Cave [GOFS kayv] in Somerset, diggers found Cheddar Man.

DNA tests on his skull showed dark skin, dark curls, and blue eyes. At Star Carr in Yorkshire, families built wooden lakeside platforms. Makers carved red-deer antler headdresses with holes for hunting disguises or dances.

[1.3] c. 6500–4000 BC: Rising Seas & the Sinking of Doggerland
“Why did flooding Doggerland turn Britain into an island around 6500 BC?”

For thousands of years, hunters walked from Europe to Britain across dry land. Historians call this green land bridge Doggerland. Families camped beside its rivers and marshes to spear eels, net ducks, and trap beavers.

Yet melting northern ice sheets kept pouring huge amounts of water into the sea. Around 6500 BC, rising waves and storms flooded low Doggerland forever. Today, fishing boats still pull mammoth teeth and flint tools from the North Sea floor. Flooding Doggerland turned Britain into an island!

STONE AGE TO IRON AGE BRITAIN (c. 800,000 BC–AD 43) LESSON 2 OF 6 • CLASSROOM READING TEXT
LESSON 2 • Change & Continuity / Archaeological Evidence

The First Farmers & Skara Brae (c. 4000–2500 BC)

Key Enquiry: How did farming and stone villages change Stone Age life?
[2.1] c. 4000–3500 BC: Boats Across the Sea & the First British Farms
“How did farming change everyday life in Britain after 4000 BC?”

Around 4000 BC, families sailed wooden boats across the sea to island Britain. Thus began the Neolithic [nee-oh-LITH-ik], or New Stone Age, when farming (agriculture) started. Settlers brought tame sheep, pigs, and cattle, plus wheat and barley seeds.

Villagers felled thick forests using smooth polished stone axes in wooden handles. Farmers planted crops and cut ripe stalks with curved flint sickles. Potters coiled wet clay into pottery bowls for hot stews. Steady harvests let families live in thatched villages all year.

[2.2] c. 3100 BC & 1850: The Storm That Uncovered Skara Brae in Orkney
“What did the 1850 storm reveal inside the stone homes of Skara Brae?”

In winter 1850, a fierce storm blew sand dunes off Orkney [ORK-nee] in northern Scotland. Underneath lay Skara Brae [SKA-ruh BRAY], a stone village built around 3100 BC! Few trees grew on windy Orkney, so villagers stacked flat coastal flagstones into eight snug homes linked by roofed passages.

Inside each house, stone box beds were once stuffed with soft heather and sheepskins. Families cooked over a central hearth, displayed treasures on a stone dresser, and even built indoor stone drains!

[2.3] c. 3650–2500 BC: Ancestor Tombs at West Kennet Long Barrow
“Why did Neolithic villagers build stone tombs like West Kennet Long Barrow?”

Settled Neolithic villagers also worked together to build giant stone tombs on high hills. Around 3650 BC, families in Wiltshire raised West Kennet Long Barrow, a long chalk mound. Heavy boulders guarded five dark stone chambers inside its entrance.

Over many years, villagers placed the bones of nearly fifty ancestors inside. Mourners left hand-coiled clay bowls, bone pins, and beads beside them. Families feasted outside, as long barrows showed everyone that their community belonged to that land.

LESSON 3 • Historical Interpretation & Significance

Secrets of Stonehenge (c. 3000–2200 BC)

Key Enquiry: How and why did Stone Age people build giant Stonehenge?
[3.1] c. 3000–2500 BC: Antler Picks, Chalk Henges & Welsh Bluestones
“How did Stonehenge begin around 3000 BC, and where did the bluestones come from?”

Families built Stonehenge on Salisbury Plain in stages over many centuries! Around 3000 BC, workers dug a round chalk ditch and bank called a henge. Using red-deer antler picks and cattle bone shovels, they chipped white chalk and buried cremated ancestors inside.

Around 2500 BC, teams hauled eighty spotted bluestones from the Preseli Hills [preh-SEL-ee] in Wales. Moving those heavy stones 140 miles across hills and rivers took plant ropes, wooden sledges, and huge teamwork!

[3.2] c. 2500 BC: 25-Tonne Sarsen Trilithons & Durrington Walls Village
“How did builders raise 25-tonne sarsen trilithons and live at Durrington Walls?”

Next came giant grey sarsen [SAR-sun] boulders, as heavy as four elephants! Without wheels or cranes, teams dragged these 25-tonne blocks twenty miles on wooden sledges and rollers. Masons pounded them smooth with stone balls.

Builders raised upright pairs and locked top lintels into three-stone trilithons [TRY-lith-onz] using mortise-and-tenon peg joints. Two miles away at Durrington Walls, workers slept in warm chalk houses and shared huge winter feasts of roast pig and cattle.

[3.3] c. 2500–2200 BC: The Heel Stone & Solstice Sun Alignments
“Why did Neolithic people align Stonehenge and the Heel Stone with the sun?”

Why did Neolithic people work without metal to raise Stonehenge and nearby Avebury? Nobody left written records, so archaeologists study buried clues and sky alignments. Outside the main circle stands a lone boulder called the Heel Stone.

At the Midsummer solstice, the rising sun shines straight over the Heel Stone into Stonehenge! At the Midwinter solstice, the setting sun glows between the tallest trilithon. Aligning the stones with the sun created a giant solar calendar and ancestor shrine.

LESSON 4 • Change & Continuity (Technology & Migration)

Enter the Bronze Age & Beaker People (c. 2500–1200 BC)

Key Enquiry: How did Beaker newcomers and bronze metal change life in Britain?
[4.1] Beaker Newcomers & Mining Metal (c. 2500–2000 BC)
“How did newcomers and miners start metalworking in Britain around 2400 BC?”

Around 2400 BC, newcomers called the Beaker people sailed from Europe to Britain. They brought bell-shaped clay beakers stamped with comb patterns. Better still, these newcomers brought metalworking skills that ended the Stone Age!

Miners crawled through tunnels at Great Orme [grayt ORM] in North Wales to dig green copper rock. In Cornwall, workers gathered heavy tin ore from streams and cliffs. Smiths crushed the rock and smelted it over hot fires until liquid metal ran free.

[4.2] Mixing Copper & Tin Into Tough Bronze (c. 2100–1500 BC)
“Why were cast bronze axes better than copper or chipped flint?”

Pure copper bent too easily against hard oak trees. Clever smiths mixed nine parts copper with one part tin to make tough golden bronze! They poured hot liquid bronze into hollow stone two-piece moulds to cast sharp axe blades.

Chipped flint snapped forever, whereas broken bronze axes could be melted down and cast again. Strong bronze axes cleared thick woodland much faster for sunny crop fields. Families guarding copper and tin trade routes soon grew rich.

[4.3] Golden Capes & The Amesbury Archer (c. 2300–1500 BC)
“What do gold treasures and the Archer near Stonehenge reveal?”

Master smiths hammered thin gold sheets into dazzling treasures for Bronze Age leaders. One Welsh ruler wore the Mold Gold Cape, while others wore crescent-moon lunulae [LOO-nyoo-lee] collars and diamond gold plates at Bush Barrow.

Near Stonehenge, diggers found the Amesbury Archer [AYMZ-bree AR-cher], buried around 2300 BC with over a hundred items. His grave held five clay beakers, copper knives, arrowheads, and gold hair rings. Chemical tests on his tooth enamel proved he grew up near the snowy Alps!

STONE AGE TO IRON AGE BRITAIN (c. 800,000 BC–AD 43) LESSON 5 OF 6 • CLASSROOM READING TEXT
LESSON 5 • Using Archaeological Evidence

Must Farm — "Britain's Pompeii" (c. 1200–800 BC)

Key Enquiry: What did the sunken village at Must Farm reveal about Bronze Age homes?
[5.1] Stilt Roundhouses & A Sudden Fire (c. 900 BC)
“Why did Must Farm earn the nickname "Britain's Pompeii"?”

Around 900 BC, Bronze Age families built wooden roundhouses at Must Farm in Cambridgeshire. Each house stood on sturdy oak stilts above a slow river. Nearby at Flag Fen, builders drove thousands of timber posts to carry a wooden causeway across marshes.

Soon after, a sudden fire swept across Must Farm's thatched roofs! Families escaped safely as burning homes dropped into the river. Thick, airless waterlogged wet mud sealed everything inside, earning Must Farm the nickname "Britain's Pompeii" [pom-PAY].

[5.2] Porridge Spoons, Cloth & Britain's Oldest Wheel
“What everyday treasures survived beneath Must Farm's wet river mud?”

On dry land, ancient wood and cloth usually rot away. Beneath Must Farm's wet river mud, diggers found amazing everyday treasures! Clay bowls still held charred porridge with a wooden spoon inside. Villagers also wove wicker eel traps from willow twigs.

Families spun soft plant-fibre cloth and slotted bronze axes into wooden handles. Best of all, diggers found a complete one-metre wooden wheel made of ash planks around 900 BC — the oldest complete wheel in Britain!

[5.3] Sacred Waters & Crossing the Channel in Oak Boats
“How did Bronze Age sailors cross the English Channel to trade?”

Tiny glass beads from Mediterranean workshops reached Must Farm by long trade routes! Meanwhile at Flag Fen, villagers lowered shiny bronze shields and swords into sacred waters as gifts.

How did Bronze Age sailors cross the choppy English Channel before iron nails existed? At Dover in Kent, diggers found the Dover Bronze Age Boat — a sewn-plank boat! Builders stitched thick oak planks together with twisted yew branches and moss, paddling tin and bronze between Britain and France.

LESSON 6 • Change, Continuity & Unit Synthesis

Iron Age Celts & Giant Hillforts (c. 800 BC–AD 43)

Key Enquiry: How did iron tools and giant hillforts shape Celtic Britain?
[6.1] Blacksmiths, Iron Ploughs & Cosy Roundhouses (c. 800–400 BC)
“How did iron tools and roundhouses change farming after 800 BC?”

Around 800 BC, smiths mastered a tough metal that began Britain's Iron Age. Common reddish iron ore lay across British hills and bogs. Blacksmiths heated iron ore in clay furnaces and hammered strong saws, swords, and ploughshares.

Iron ploughs sliced heavy clay soil so Celtic farmers grew bumper wheat crops. Families spun a stone rotary quern [KWURN] to grind grain into flour. They lived in thatched roundhouses with wattle-and-daub walls, weaving bright wool on upright looms.

[6.2] Celtic Tribes & Giant Hillforts Like Maiden Castle (c. 400–100 BC)
“Why did rival Celtic tribes build giant hillforts across Britain?”

Richer harvests helped Britain's population grow, and rival Celtic tribes competed for cattle and land. Tribes built giant hillforts on high ridges ringed by steep earth ramparts and ditches. At Maiden Castle in Dorset, chalk banks rose like huge waves.

Winding gates forced raiders past defenders armed with smooth river slingshot stones. Inside, villagers stored grain in pits and forged red-hot iron. In Oxfordshire, tribes carved the giant Uffington White Horse into bright white hillside chalk!

[6.3] Twisted Gold Torcs, Coins & Rome Arrives (c. 100 BC–AD 43)
“What do gold treasures and coins prove about Britain before AD 43?”

Wise priests called Druids memorised sacred laws, while smiths twisted gold wires into heavy torcs like the Snettisham Great Torc [SNET-ish-um]! Makers also beat bronze horned helmets and shields as gifts for the River Thames.

By 50 BC, rulers stamped galloping horses onto gold stater coins and traded with Gaul and Rome. Then in AD 43, Emperor Claudius [KLAW-dee-us] sent four Roman legions to invade! Over 800,000 years of British prehistory ended as written history began.

Lesson 1: Ice Age Hunters & Sunken Doggerland (c. 800,000–4000 BC)

  3. Inside which deep limestone caves did Old Stone Age hunters shelter from freezing Ice Age winds?
  4. What do historians call the clever skill of striking flint rocks to chip off sharp stone flakes?
  5. Besides meat to eat, what else did one giant woolly mammoth give an Ice Age family?
Lesson 2: The First Farmers & Skara Brae (c. 4000–2500 BC)
  1. Around 4000 BC, how did Britain's first farmers bring tame sheep, cattle, and grain seeds to our island?
  2. What does the word "Neolithic" mean to historians?
  3. Which tame farm animals and grain crops did Neolithic settlers introduce to Britain around 4000 BC?
  4. Why did Neolithic craftworkers rub stone axeheads smooth on wet sandstone?
  5. Which curved flint tool did Neolithic farmers use to slice ripe stalks of wheat and barley?
Lesson 3: Secrets of Stonehenge (c. 3000–2200 BC)
  1. How did Stonehenge first begin on Salisbury Plain around 3000 BC?
  2. Which natural tools did Neolithic workers use to chip white chalk for Stonehenge's ditch?
  3. Who did Neolithic families bury inside holes around Stonehenge's early chalk ring?
  4. From which Welsh hills did teams haul eighty spotted bluestones around 2500 BC?
  5. Roughly how far did Neolithic teams drag and float the Welsh bluestones to reach Wiltshire?
Lesson 4: Enter the Bronze Age & Beaker People (c. 2500–1200 BC)
  1. Why did archaeologists name the newcomers of around 2400 BC the "Beaker people"?
  2. What game-changing skill did the Beaker newcomers bring across the sea to Britain?
  3. Where in North Wales did Bronze Age miners crawl through dark tunnels to dig green copper rock?
  4. In which part of south-west Britain did workers gather heavy tin ore from streams and cliffs?
  5. What does the word "smelting" mean in Bronze Age metalworking?
Lesson 5: Must Farm — "Britain's Pompeii" (c. 1200–800 BC)
  1. How were the Bronze Age wooden roundhouses at Must Farm built around 900 BC?
  2. What did Bronze Age builders construct across the wet marshes nearby at Flag Fen?
  3. What sudden disaster struck Must Farm less than a year after the stilt houses were built?
  4. Why did wood, cloth, and food at Must Farm NOT rot away over 3,000 years?
  5. Which famous nickname did archaeologists give Must Farm because everyday life was frozen in a single moment?
Lesson 6: Iron Age Celts & Giant Hillforts (c. 800 BC–AD 43)
  1. Around 800 BC, why could local blacksmiths make iron tools in almost every part of Britain?
  2. How did Iron Age blacksmiths turn reddish iron ore into tough saws, swords, and ploughshares?
  3. How did iron-tipped ploughshares help Celtic farming families grow bigger wheat harvests?
  4. Which clever spinning stone tool did Iron Age families turn inside roundhouses to grind grain into flour?
  5. How were the circular walls and tall roofs of cosy Iron Age roundhouses built?

KEY STAGE 2 ILLUSTRATED GLOSSARY SYLLABLE HELPERS & DEFINITIONS

Historian's Word Bank (24 Essential Terms)

Clap the italic syllables out loud together to master prehistoric archaeological words!

Prehistory Pre-his-to-ry
The vast stretch of human history before people wrote down words, dates, or stories.
Palaeolithic Pa-lae-o-lith-ic
The Old Stone Age (c. 850,000–10,000 BC), when Ice Age hunters sheltered in caves and chipped flint handaxes.
Knapping Knap-ping
Striking flint stones carefully to chip off razor-sharp flakes for handaxes, scrapers, and spear tips.
Mesolithic Mes-o-lith-ic
The Middle Stone Age (c. 10,000–4000 BC), when warming forests spread across Britain after the Ice Age.
Neolithic Ne-o-lith-ic
The New Stone Age (c. 4000–2500 BC), when Britain’s first farmers cleared woods, grew crops, and built permanent villages.
Agriculture Ag-ri-cul-ture
Farming the land by planting crops like wheat and barley and keeping tame animals such as sheep, pigs, and cattle.
Sickle Sick-le
A curved harvesting tool with a sharp chipped flint blade used to slice ripe stalks of wheat and barley.
Skara Brae Ska-ra Brae
A remarkably preserved 5,000-year-old Neolithic stone village on Orkney in Scotland, uncovered by a storm in 1850.
Henge Henge
A circular prehistoric monument framed by a wide dug-out earth ditch inside a raised outer bank.
Bluestones Blue-stones
Smaller spotted volcanic stones hauled 140 miles from the Preseli Hills in Wales to stand inside Stonehenge.
Sarsen Sar-sen
Massive, rock-hard grey sandstone boulders dragged across Wiltshire on wooden rollers to build Stonehenge’s tallest circle.
Trilithon Tri-li-thon
A giant three-stone arch formed by two tall upright boulders supporting one horizontal lintel stone locked on top.
Beaker Bea-ker
A tall, bell-shaped clay drinking pot decorated with comb patterns, brought to Britain by newcomers around 2400 BC.
Smelting Smelt-ing
Heating crushed metal-bearing rock in a fierce charcoal fire until shiny liquid metal melts out of the stone.
Bronze Bronze
A tough golden metal made by melting nine parts copper together with one part tin.
Mould Mould
A hollow two-piece stone or metal shape into which smiths poured glowing liquid bronze to cast tools.
Stilts Stilts
Tall, sturdy wooden oak posts hammered into a riverbed to hold houses safely up above the water.
Causeway Cause-way
A raised wooden bridge road built on thousands of timber posts to cross wet, boggy marshes.
Waterlogged Wa-ter-logged
Soaked completely full of water and thick mud with no air inside, stopping wood and cloth from rotting.
Wicker Wick-er
Bendy willow twigs woven neatly together to make strong baskets, walls, and funnel-shaped eel traps.
Iron ore I-ron ore
Common reddish rock dug from hills and bogs that blacksmiths heated in clay furnaces to hammer tough iron.
Rotary quern Ro-ta-ry quern
Two heavy round stones spun with a wooden handle to grind wheat and barley grains quickly into flour.
Roundhouse Round-house
A circular Iron Age family home with woven wattle-and-daub walls, a central fire, and a tall cone-shaped thatched roof.
Hillfort Hill-fort
A giant hilltop town ringed by towering earth ramparts, deep ditches, and wooden gates to guard a Celtic tribe.

MASTER CHRONOLOGICAL SPINE c. 850,000 BC TO AD 43

10 Turning Points From Ice Age Flint to Iron Age Hillforts

c. 850,000 BC
Happisburgh Footprints & Handaxes: Early Palaeolithic humans walk across dry land from Europe into Norfolk and flake teardrop flint handaxes.
c. 9000 BC
Star Carr & Cheddar Man (Mesolithic): After Ice Age glaciers melt, woodland hunters build Britain’s oldest timber house and carve 21 red-deer antler masks.
c. 6500 BC
Doggerland Floods Beneath the Sea: Rising meltwater and a giant tsunami drown the grassy land bridge of Doggerland, turning Britain into an island.
c. 4000 BC
Neolithic Farming Revolution: Newcomers bring wheat, barley, sheep, and cattle by boat, felling woods with polished stone axes and coiling clay pots.
c. 3100 BC
Stone Houses at Skara Brae, Orkney: Treeless Orkney islanders build eight snug stone houses with central hearths, box beds, dressers, and drains.
c. 3000–2500 BC
Stonehenge & Durrington Walls: Communities haul Welsh bluestones 150 miles and raise 25-tonne sarsen trilithons aligned with the Solstice sun.
c. 2300 BC
Beakers & The Amesbury Archer: An Alpine-born traveller is buried near Stonehenge with 100+ items as copper and Cornish tin launch the Bronze Age.
c. 1900–1550 BC
Mold Gold Cape & Dover Sea Boat: Master goldsmiths beat one Welsh gold ingot into a cape while stitched oak boats trade metals across the Channel.
c. 850 BC
Must Farm ("Britain’s Pompeii"): Burnt stilt houses sink into oxygen-free Fen mud, saving Britain’s oldest wheel, woven cloth, and porridge bowls!
c. 800 BC–AD 43
Iron Age Celts & Maiden Castle: Iron ploughs, thatched roundhouses, Snettisham gold torcs, and giant hillforts flourish until Rome invades in AD 43.
Big Picture Historian Discussion

1. Myth-Busting: How do Skara Brae's stone dressers, Stonehenge's Lego-like joints, Must Farm's fine woven cloth, and Snettisham gold torcs smash the myth of "clumsy cavemen"?
2. Next Stop — Roman Britain (AD 43): When Emperor Claudius's legions land in Kent in AD 43, what strengths—and what weaknesses—will Iron Age Celtic tribes face?
